titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §170–177: the slave-woman’s sons and the widow (xxviii 38 – xxx 60)
part: Laws §170–177 · slave-woman’s sons, widows & slave marriages (Col. xxviii 38 – xxx 60)
about: Eight laws on children of unequal mothers and on the position of a woman who outlives her husband. If a father has called his slave-woman’s sons “my sons”, they divide his estate equally with the sons of his wife, and the heir, the wife’s son, chooses from the share (§170); if he never did, they do not share, but they and their mother are to be set free; the wife, once widowed, takes her dowry and the marriage-gift her husband wrote out for her, lives on in his house, and her estate goes to her sons alone (§171). If her husband never gave a marriage-gift, her dowry is made good to her and she takes a share like one heir’s, and her sons may not drive her out if the judges find them in the wrong (§172). If she chooses to leave, she leaves the marriage-gift to her sons, takes her father’s-house dowry, and marries the man of her choice (§172A). If she marries again and has children, all her children, from both marriages, divide her dowry; if she has none by the later husband, her dowry goes to the sons of her “ḫāwirum”, probably her first husband (§173–174). Then come free women married to slaves, of the palace or of a commoner: the slave’s owner may not claim her children as slaves (§175), and when the slave dies, what the couple acquired is halved between his owner and the woman, who takes her own dowry out first and takes her half for her sons (§176–176A). The last law protects a widow’s young sons: she may not remarry without the judges, who look into the property of her first husband’s house and have the couple leave a tablet; the household goods may not be sold, and a buyer loses his silver (§177). Harper’s transliteration writes the Sumerian signs for ‘son’, ‘slave-woman’, ‘house’ and ‘silver’ as Akkadian words, and each was checked on the plate; the few doubtful spellings are marked in the notes.

sentences.l: If a-man his-wife sons has-borne-him and his-slave-woman sons has-borne-him,
sentences.i: If a man’s wife has borne him sons, and his slave-woman has borne him sons,
sentences.n: A long law with a long “if”, so read it clause by clause; this unit is the first half of the protasis. šumma awīlum opens it as always. ḫīrtašu is “his wife”: ḫīrtum (Harper: “wife”) is the free wife, set here against the slave-woman. mārī ūlissum is “sons she bore him”: mārī is DUMU with the two plural signs (DUMU{meš}, the plural signs silent), and ūlissum is walādum “to bear” + -šum “to him”, the d of ūlid and the š of -šum merging into ss, as at §167; the last sign, ZUM, is one complex sign, its identification UNCERTAIN, as there. u is the conjunction (the sign U3, “and”). amassu is “his slave-woman”: GEME₂ is two signs (SAL and KUR) and ZU writes -ssu (amat + -šu); Harper prints ama-zu. Slave-woman and wife each bear sons, and the rest of the law is about how those sons divide the father’s estate.

sentences.l: the-father in-his-lifetime to-the-sons whom the-slave-woman bore-him ‘my-sons’ has-said, with the-sons of-the-wife has-counted-them,
sentences.i: and the father, in his lifetime, has said “my sons” to the sons the slave-woman bore him and has counted them with the sons of the wife,
sentences.n: The father has acknowledged the slave-woman’s sons. ina bultišu is “in his lifetime”: bultum is Harper’s BULTU “life-time” (the root is balāṭum “to live”, so modern editions write bulṭu; Harper prints ti). ana mārī ša amtum ūlidušum is “to the sons whom the slave-woman bore him”: ša “which” opens a relative clause whose subject, amtum, comes first, in the nominative, with the verb last in the subjunctive -u before -šum “to him”; Harper’s ul-du-šum is a shortened spelling, so the vowels of ūlidušum are UNCERTAIN, as at §119 and §137–138. mārūa iqtabi is “‘my sons’ he has said”: mārūa is DUMU{meš}, then the signs U and A, “my sons”, and iqtabi is the perfect of qabûm “to say”, as at §159. itti mārī ḫīrtim is “with the sons of the wife”. imtanūšunūti is manûm “to count” (not the manûm “mina”) in the perfect + šunūti “them”: “he has counted them”; read from the spelling im-ta-nu-šu-nu-ti, its vowels UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: after the-father to-fate has-gone, from the-property of-the-house of-the-father the-sons of-the-wife and the-sons of-the-slave-woman equally they-shall-divide,
sentences.i: After the father has gone to his fate, the sons of the wife and the sons of the slave-woman shall divide the property of the father’s house equally.
sentences.n: The ruling: acknowledged sons share equally. warka abum ana šīmtim ittalku is “after the father has gone to his fate”: warka “after”, šīmtim “fate”, and ittalku the perfect of alākum “to go” with the subjunctive -u (the same idiom as at §165–167). ina makkūr bīt abim is “from the property of the father’s house”: makkūr is a Sumerogram Harper reads ŠA.GA (two signs, GAR and GA), bīt is É, and a-ba is Harper’s spelling of abim “of the father”, UNCERTAIN, as at §158. The sons of the wife (mārū ḫīrtim) and the sons of the slave-woman (mārū amtim, GEME₂ with no ending written) divide mitḫāriš “equally”, izuzzū “they shall divide” (zâzum, as at §165). DUMU{meš} does not show the case: as the subject of izuzzū the plural is the nominative mārū, where the genitive and accusative are mārī.

sentences.l: the-heir, the-son of-the-wife, from the-share he-shall-choose-and he-shall-take.
sentences.i: The heir, the son of the wife, shall choose from the share and take it.
sentences.n: A privilege for the senior son. DUMU.UŠ is two signs, DUMU and UŠ; I read it aplum “heir” (Harper prints TUR.UŠ and reads ablu; whether the title means “heir” or simply “eldest son” is not certain, UNCERTAIN). After it comes mār ḫīrtim “the son of the wife”, DUMU again, in apposition. ina zittim is “from the share” (zittum, as at §137 and §166, here spelled zi-it-tim; the plate row is crowded and I could not match every stroke group to a sign, so the spelling is UNCERTAIN and Harper’s reading is followed). inassaqma is nasāqum “to choose, select” + -ma “and”: the present, “he shall choose, and”, the same word as at §60 (Harper’s i-na-za-ak-ma, ZA for sa and AK for aq); ileqqi “he shall take”. The text does not say what he chooses or in what order, only that he chooses from the share and takes it (UNCERTAIN).

sentences.l: And if the-father in-his-lifetime to-the-sons whom the-slave-woman bore-him ‘my-sons’ not has-said,
sentences.i: And if the father, in his lifetime, has not said “my sons” to the sons the slave-woman bore him,
sentences.n: The opposite case, built on §170 word for word. u šumma is “and if” (the conjunction written with U3, then šumma). The clause is §170’s, with lā “not” before iqtabi: lā iqtabi “he has not said”. If the father never called the slave-woman’s sons “my sons”, the rest of the law gives their different position.

sentences.l: after the-father to-fate has-gone, from the-property of-the-house of-the-father the-sons of-the-slave-woman with the-sons of-the-wife not they-shall-divide,
sentences.i: after the father has gone to his fate, the sons of the slave-woman shall not divide the property of the father’s house with the sons of the wife.
sentences.n: The same words as §170, with the negative: ul izuzzū “they shall not divide” (ul, the signs U and UL, then the present plural of zâzum). The sons of the slave-woman, not acknowledged in the father’s lifetime, get no share beside the sons of the wife; itti “with” puts the two groups side by side.

sentences.l: the-release of-the-slave-woman and her-sons shall-be-set; the-sons of-the-wife against the-sons of-the-slave-woman for slavery not they-shall-claim.
sentences.i: But the release of the slave-woman and of her sons shall be established; the sons of the wife shall not lay claim against the sons of the slave-woman for slavery.
sentences.n: What the slave-woman’s sons do get: freedom. andurār amtim u mārīša is “the release of the slave-woman and of her sons”: andurārum is release (Harper: “freedom”; the word of §117, andurāršunu), here in the construct, with the genitive amtim and the two linked by u. iššakkan is the N-stem present of šakānum, “shall be set, shall be established” (the passive; as at §105 and §117). Harper prints iš-ta-ak-ka-an and lists it among the perfects (his I, 2); I keep his spelling in the reading and normalize to the passive present the sense needs, UNCERTAIN. The second half: mārū ḫīrtim ana mārī amtim ana wardūtim ul iraggumū is “the sons of the wife against the sons of the slave-woman for slavery shall not claim”: ragāmum “to claim” (plural iraggumū; the singular iraggum is at §162–163), wardūtim “slavery” (spelled wa-ar-du-tim) after ana “for”.

sentences.l: the-wife her-dowry and the-marriage-gift which her-husband gave-her, on a-tablet wrote-for-her, she-shall-take-and,
sentences.i: the wife shall take her dowry and the marriage-gift that her husband gave her and wrote out for her on a tablet, and
sentences.n: The wife’s own property. ḫīrtum šeriqtaša is “the wife, her dowry”; šeriqtum is what the bride brings from her father’s house (§138). nudunnam is the marriage-gift (Harper’s NUDUNNU: “gift from groom to bride at marriage”); Harper prints nu-du-na-am here and nu-du-un-na-am at §172, the same word. ša mussa iddinušim is “which her husband gave her”: iddinu + -šim “to her”, the subjunctive -u short before -šim (the house rule), and mussa as at §153. ina ṭuppim išṭurušim is “on a tablet he wrote for her”: ṭuppum “tablet” (Harper’s dub-bi-im) and the same relative construction with šaṭārum “to write”. ileqqēma is “she shall take, and”: leqûm + -ma, as at §165.

sentences.l: in the-dwelling of-her-husband she-shall-dwell; as-long-as she-lives she-shall-eat; for silver not she-shall-give; her-estate of-her-sons-only.
sentences.i: She shall live in her husband’s house; as long as she lives she shall have the use of it; she shall not give it for silver; her estate belongs to her sons alone.
sentences.n: What she may do with it. ina šubat mutiša uššab is “in the dwelling of her husband she shall dwell” (šubtum, wašābum “to sit, dwell”). adi balṭat ikkal is “as long as she lives she shall eat”: adi “as long as”, balṭat the stative of balāṭum “to live”, ikkal the present of akālum “to eat”; no object is written, and “to eat” is read as “to have the use of” what she took, UNCERTAIN. ana kaspim ul inaddin is “for silver she shall not give”, that is, she may not sell it. warkassa ša mārīša-ma is “her estate (is) of her sons only”: warkatum is “what is behind”; with -ša “her” it is “her estate”, what she leaves, the sense “her case” at §172 resting on context, UNCERTAIN; ša “of” and -ma “only”, so the property passes to her own children.

sentences.l: If her-husband a-marriage-gift not has-given-her, her-dowry has-made-good-to-her-and,
sentences.i: If her husband has not given her a marriage-gift, but has made good her dowry to her,
sentences.n: Another widow’s case: a husband who never gave the marriage-gift. mussa nudunnam lā iddiššim is “her husband a marriage-gift has not given her”: iddiššim is iddin + -šim, the n and š merged (id-di-iš-ši-im). šeriqtaša ušallamšimma is “her dowry he has made good to her, and”: ušallam is the D-stem of šalāmum “to be whole”, “to make good, to restore” (Harper’s “to make good”) with -šim “to her” and -ma “and”. Harper prints u-ša-la-mu-ši-im-ma, with an extra MU after LA (his glossary has the same spelling); the form wanted is ušallamšimma, as at §138, §149 and §156 (u-ša-lam-ši-im-ma), and I read the MU as a spelling of the am, UNCERTAIN. The sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.l: from the-property of-the-house of-her-husband a-share like one heir she-shall-take.
sentences.i: she shall take a share from the property of her husband’s house, like one heir.
sentences.n: The apodosis: she receives a child’s share. ina makkūr bīt mutiša is “from the property of the house of her husband” (ŠA.GA and É, as at §170). zittam is “a share” (Harper’s ṣi-it-tam, with ṣ); kīma aplim ištēn is “like one heir”: aplim is spelled ab-lim (the sign AB read ab or ap; Harper’s ablim), “of an heir”, and ištēn “one”. So the widow takes an heir’s portion (the same phrase as at §137).

sentences.l: If her-sons in-order-to from-the-house the-making-go-out scheme-against-her, the-judges her-case shall-investigate-and, the-sons guilt have-laid,
sentences.i: If her sons scheme against her in order to make her leave the house, the judges shall investigate her case, and if the sons are in the wrong,
sentences.n: When the sons try to push her out. aššum ina bītim šūṣîm is “in order to make (her) go out of the house”: aššum “in order to”, bītim (É) “the house”, šūṣîm the Š infinitive of waṣûm “to go out” (Harper’s šu-zi-im, ZI read ṣi). uzaḫḫamūši is the D present plural of zaḫāmum + -ši “her”; Harper’s glossary gives “to scheme”, so “they scheme against her”, UNCERTAIN. dajjānū warkassa iparrasūma is “the judges her case shall investigate, and” (warkassa “her case”, as the unit at §168 had warkassu; iparrasūma as there, “they shall investigate”). mārū arnam immidū is “the sons guilt have laid”: emēdum “to lay on”, with arnam “guilt” (Harper’s glossary: “to be in the wrong, to have blame”). The protasis ends here; the next unit gives the ruling.

sentences.l: that woman from the-house of-her-husband not shall-go-out.
sentences.i: that woman shall not leave her husband’s house.
sentences.n: The ruling: zinništum šī “that woman” (SAL alone, šī as at §163). ina bīt mutiša ul uṣṣi is “from her husband’s house she shall not go out”: uṣṣi is the present of waṣûm, written uz-zi (the signs UZ and ZI, ṣṣ doubled). The widow cannot be driven out if the sons are in the wrong.

sentences.l: If that woman to the-going-out her-face has-set, the-marriage-gift which her-husband gave-her to-her-sons she-shall-leave,
sentences.i: If that woman has set her face to go out, she shall leave to her sons the marriage-gift that her husband gave her;
sentences.n: Harper gives this its own heading, §172A; the chips number the laws, so it carries no § mark of its own and continues §172 (as §133A did). ana wuṣîm panīša ištakan is “to going out her face she has set”, the idiom for making up one’s mind (§141–152): wuṣîm is the infinitive of waṣûm (Harper’s wa-ṣi-im), panīša “her face” (pānum + -ša), ištakan the perfect of šakānum. The rest repeats the marriage-gift clause of §171: nudunnam ša mussa iddinušim “the marriage-gift which her husband gave her”. ana mārīša izzib is “to her sons she shall leave (it)”: izzib is the present of ezēbum “to leave behind”, as at §138. A widow who goes leaves the husband’s marriage-gift to her sons.

sentences.l: the-dowry of-the-house of-her-father she-shall-take-and, the-husband of-her-heart shall-take-her.
sentences.i: She shall take the dowry of her father’s house, and the husband of her heart shall take her.
sentences.n: What she takes with her: šeriqtam ša bīt abiša is “the dowry of the house of her father” (abiša, a-bi-ša, “her father’s”), taken ileqqēma “she shall take, and”. mut libbiša iḫḫazzi is “the husband of her heart shall take her”: mut libbiša, spelled mu-ut li-ib-bi-ša, is the man she chooses (as at §137), and iḫḫazzi is aḫāzum “to take (as wife)” + -ši “her”, written i-iḫ-ḫa-az-zi (the house spelling of §137 and §156).

sentences.l: If that-woman where she-entered to her-husband the-later children has-borne, after that-woman has-died,
sentences.i: If that woman has borne children to her later husband, in the place where she entered, and after that woman has died,
sentences.n: Two marriages, two sets of children. šumma zinništum šī is “if that woman” (SAL alone, as at §163). ašar īrubu is “where she entered”, the new household: ašar “where”, īrubu the preterite of erēbum “to enter” with the subjunctive -u. ana mutiša warkîm is “to her later husband”: warkûm is “later, subsequent”, in the genitive after mutiša, spelled wa-ar-ki-im. mārī ittalad is “children she has borne”: ittalad is the perfect of walādum “to bear” (§135, §146, §167), with no subject written. warka zinništum šī imtūt is “after that woman has died”: warka “after” (the word of §170), imtūt the perfect of mâtum “to die” (§115).

sentences.l: her-dowry the-former children and the-later ones shall-divide.
sentences.i: her former and her later children shall divide her dowry.
sentences.n: The ruling: the dowry is shared by the children of both marriages. šeriqtaša “her dowry” comes first, as the object. mārū maḫrūtum u warkūtum is “the children, the former and the later”: mārū is the nominative plural (the subject of izuzzū); maḫrûm “first, former” and warkûm “later” stand as plural forms in -ūtum (spelled maḫ-ru-tum, wa-ar-ku-tum); izuzzū “they shall divide”, as at §170.

sentences.l: If to her-husband the-later children not she-has-borne, her-dowry the-sons of-her-ḫāwirum-only shall-take.
sentences.i: If she has not borne children to her later husband, only the sons of her first husband (?) shall take her dowry.
sentences.n: The other case: no children by the later husband. šumma ana mutiša warkîm mārī lā ittalad is “if to her later husband children she has not borne”, the clause of §173 with lā. mārū ḫāwirīšama ileqqû is “the sons of her ḫāwirum only shall take”: ḫāwirum is a rarer word for “husband” (Harper: “groom, husband”; at §135 it is the first husband), -ša “her”, -ma “only”; set against “later husband” above it points to her first husband, UNCERTAIN, so the i marks it (?). ileqqû is the plural present of leqûm (the signs QU and U), “they shall take”.

sentences.l: If either a-slave of-the-palace or a-slave of-a-commoner the-daughter of-a-man has-taken-and children she-has-borne,
sentences.i: If either a slave of the palace or a slave of a commoner has taken a man’s daughter, and she has borne children,
sentences.n: A free woman married to a slave. lū warad ekallim u lū warad muškēnim is “either a slave of the palace or a slave of a commoner”: lū … u lū “either … or” (the sign LU); warad is wardum “slave” in the construct, written with the sign ARAD and no ending, and ekallim is É.GAL “palace”, genitive; muškēnim is the genitive of muškēnum, “commoner”, MAŠ.EN.KAK (three signs). mārat awīlim is “the daughter of a man” (DUMU.SAL, two signs, then a-wi-lim). iḫuzma is “he has taken (her as wife)”: aḫāzum + -ma “and”. mārī ittalad is “children she has borne”, as at §173. The slave is the subject of iḫuzma, the woman of ittalad.

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-slave to-the-children of-the-daughter of-a-man for slavery not shall-claim.
sentences.i: the slave’s owner shall not lay claim to the children of the man’s daughter for slavery.
sentences.n: The ruling: the children are free. bēl wardim is “the owner of the slave” (be-el, then ARAD with no ending written, wardim). ana mārī mārat awīlim ana wardūtim ul iraggum is “to the children of the man’s daughter for slavery he shall not claim”: ragāmum “to claim”, iraggum the singular present (the plural at §171 was iraggumū; compare §162–163 iraggum), wardūtim “slavery”. Harper prints a-ṇa with a dot under the n at XXIX 65; it is a spot of type, not a sign.

sentences.l: And if a-slave of-the-palace or a-slave of-a-commoner the-daughter of-a-man has-taken-and,
sentences.i: And if a slave of the palace or a slave of a commoner has taken a man’s daughter, and
sentences.n: The next case, built on §175: u šumma “and if”, then the same subject, object and verb: warad ekallim u lū warad muškēnim “a slave of the palace or a slave of a commoner”, mārat awīlim “a man’s daughter”, iḫuzma “he has taken (her), and”. The protasis goes on through the next two units.

sentences.l: when he-took-her, together-with the-dowry of-the-house of-her-father into the-house of-the-slave of-the-palace or of-a-slave of-a-commoner she-entered-and,
sentences.i: when he took her, and she entered the house of the slave of the palace or of the slave of the commoner together with the dowry of her father’s house,
sentences.n: inūma iḫuzuši is “when he took her”: inūma “when” (as at §165), iḫuzuši the preterite of aḫāzum with the subjunctive -u before -ši “her”; the -u is short here because the subject is one slave (house rule), UNCERTAIN, since the spelling i-ḫu-zu-ši does not show the length. gadum šeriqtim ša bīt abiša is “together with the dowry of her father’s house”: gadum “together with” (Harper’s GADU, “together, with”). ana bīt warad ekallim u lū warad muškēnim īrubma is “into the house of the slave of the palace or of a slave of a commoner she entered, and”: īrubma is the preterite of erēbum “to enter” + -ma. The dowry she brings in goes into the slave’s house with her.

sentences.l: since they-were-joined a-house they-made, property they-acquired, afterwards the-slave of-the-palace or the-slave of-a-commoner to-fate has-gone,
sentences.i: and since they were joined they have made a house and acquired property, and afterwards the slave of the palace or the slave of the commoner has gone to his fate,
sentences.n: ištu innemdū is “since they were joined”: ištu “since, after”, innemdū the N-stem preterite plural of emēdum “to lay on”, “to be joined together” (Harper: “to join hands”, his IV, 1), here the couple. bītam īpušū is “a house they made” (epēšum “to do, make”; īpušū the preterite plural with the subjunctive; bītam is É with no ending written); bīšam iršû is “property they acquired”: bīšum is Harper’s BISU, “property, possessions”, and iršû the preterite plural of rašûm “to acquire” (Harper’s ir-su-u). warkānumma is “afterwards, and”, as at §155. The slave then ana šīmtim ittalak “has gone to his fate”: the perfect, not the subjunctive of §170.

sentences.l: the-daughter of-a-man her-dowry shall-take, and whatever of-her-husband and of-her since they-were-joined they-acquired,
sentences.i: the man’s daughter shall take her dowry, and whatever she and her husband have acquired since they were joined
sentences.n: The ruling begins: mārat awīlim šeriqtaša ileqqi “the man’s daughter shall take her dowry”, the dowry she brought in with her. u mimma ša mussa u šī ištu innemdū iršû is “and whatever, of her husband and of her, since they were joined they acquired”: mimma “whatever”, ša mussa u šī “that is her husband’s and hers” (šī “she”, as at §163), the same clause as the previous unit’s ištu innemdū … iršû. The sentence continues in the next unit with what happens to that shared property.

sentences.l: into-its-two they-shall-divide-and, half the-owner of-the-slave shall-take, half the-daughter of-a-man for her-sons shall-take.
sentences.i: they shall divide it into two parts; the slave’s owner shall take one half, and the man’s daughter shall take the other half for her sons.
sentences.n: The shared property is halved. ana šinīšu izuzzūma is “into its two they shall divide, and”: šinā “two” + -šu “its”, “into two parts”, izuzzūma the present plural of zâzum + -ma. mišlam bēl wardim ileqqi is “half the owner of the slave shall take”: mišlum “half” in the accusative, then ileqqi “he shall take”; mišlam mārat awīlim ana mārīša ileqqi is “half the man’s daughter for her sons shall take”. So the dead slave’s owner (the palace or the commoner) gets half of what the couple acquired, and the woman, for her children, the other half; her dowry was settled in the previous unit.

sentences.l: If the-daughter of-a-man a-dowry not has, whatever of-her-husband and of-her since they-were-joined they-acquired,
sentences.i: If a man’s daughter has no dowry, whatever she and her husband have acquired since they were joined
sentences.n: Harper’s own heading §176A: the same case with a woman who had no dowry, so no § chip of its own. šeriqtam lā īšu is “a dowry he/she has not” (īšu the preterite of išûm “to have”, as at §142 lā īšu); the rest is the clause of §176 just before: mimma ša mussa u šī ištu innemdū iršû “whatever of her husband and of her since they were joined they acquired”. The ruling follows in the next unit.

sentences.l: into-its-two they-shall-divide-and, half the-owner of-the-slave shall-take, half the-daughter of-a-man for her-sons shall-take.
sentences.i: they shall divide it into two parts; the slave’s owner shall take one half, and the man’s daughter shall take the other half for her sons.
sentences.n: The ruling repeats §176 word for word: the property they acquired together is divided in two, half to the slave’s owner, half to the woman for her sons. The difference from §176 is only that she brought no dowry of her own to take out first.

sentences.l: If a-widow whose children are-small to another house to-enter her-face has-set, without the-judges not she-shall-enter.
sentences.i: If a widow whose children are young has set her face to enter another house, she shall not enter without the judges.
sentences.n: A widow with young children. NU.MU.SU is three signs (NU, MU, SU), the logogram for “widow”, which I read almattum (Harper prints it as the sign-group only; the reading is the standard one for this group). ša mārūša ṣiḫḫirū is “whose children are small” (mārūša, the nominative plural, as the subject of the small ones): ṣiḫḫirū is a plural form of ṣeḫrum “small” (Harper: ṣi-iḫ-ḫi-ru), UNCERTAIN in its ending. ana bītim šanîm erēbim panīša ištakan is “to another house to enter her face she has set”, the same idiom as at §172A, with erēbim the infinitive of erēbum “to enter”. balum dajjānī ul irrub is “without the judges she shall not enter”: balum “without”, dajjānī the genitive plural of dajjānum “judge”, and irrub the present of erēbum (§134).

sentences.l: When to another house she-enters, the-judges the-estate of-the-house of-her-husband the-former shall-investigate-and,
sentences.i: When she enters another house, the judges shall investigate the estate of her former husband’s house, and
sentences.n: inūma ana bītim šanîm irrubu is “when to another house she enters”: inūma “when”, irrubu the present with the subjunctive -u (spelled i-ir-ru-bu, as at §141–152). dajjānū warkat bīt mutiša panîm iparrasūma is “the judges the estate of the house of her husband, the former, shall investigate, and”: warkat is the construct of warkatum (here the estate, the circumstances of the house; compare warkassa at §171–172), and panîm is panûm “former, earlier”, agreeing with mutiša (spelled pa-ni-im), “her former husband”. The judges therefore first examine the first husband’s house.

sentences.l: the-house of her-former husband to her-later husband and that woman they-shall-entrust-and a-tablet they-shall-make-leave-them.
sentences.i: they shall entrust the house of her former husband to her later husband and to that woman, and have them leave a tablet.
sentences.n: The judges hand the former husband’s house over. bītam ša mutiša panîm is “the house of her former husband”; ana mutiša warkîm u zinništim šuāti is “to her later husband and to that woman” (SAL alone, šuāti “that”). ipaqqidūma is the present plural of paqādum “to entrust” + -ma “and”. ṭuppam ušezzibūšunūti is “a tablet they shall have them leave”: ṭuppam “tablet” (dup-pa-am), ušezzibū the Š-stem present plural of ezēbum “to leave” (u-še-iz-zi-bu), šunūti “them”; as at §151 (ṭuppam uštēzib) the sense is to have a tablet left as a record, UNCERTAIN. The tablet records what was handed over.

sentences.l: the-house they-shall-guard and the-small-ones they-shall-raise; the-household-goods for silver not they-shall-give.
sentences.i: They shall look after the house and bring up the young children; they shall not sell the household goods.
sentences.n: What the couple must do: bītam inaṣṣarū is “the house they shall guard” (naṣārum, inaṣṣarū the present plural); ṣiḫḫirūtim urabbû is “the small ones they shall raise” (rabûm, D-stem, “to bring up”, as at §137; ṣiḫḫirūtim, spelled ṣi-iḫ-ḫi-ru-tim, is the small children). unīātim is Harper’s UNUTU, “household goods” (u-ni-a-tim, the plural, a different spelling of the unūt of the next unit). ana kaspim ul inaddinū is “for silver they shall not give”, i.e. they shall not sell them; the verb is plural (inaddinū), as the couple are the subject.

sentences.l: The-buyer who the-household-goods of-the-sons of-the-widow buys, from his-silver shall-lose, the-property to its-owner shall-return.
sentences.i: The buyer who buys the household goods of the widow’s sons shall forfeit his silver; the property shall return to its owner.
sentences.n: The penalty for buying them. šayyāmānum is “the buyer” (as at §9–10). ša unūt mārī almattim išammu is “who the household goods of the sons of the widow buys”: unūt is the construct of unūtum, išammu the present of šâmum “to buy”, with the subjunctive -u (spelled i-ša-am-mu; not the šâmum “to fix”). ina kaspišu ītelli is “from his silver he shall lose”, the house wording “he forfeits his silver” (§112–126 ītelli). makkūr ana bēlišu itâr is “the property to its owner shall return”: makkūr is again ŠA.GA (Harper prints ŠA.GA. with a period after GA at XXX 59), bēlišu “its owner” (be-li-šu), itâr the present of târum “to return”, as at §131 and §135–136. The buyer loses both goods and silver; the widow’s sons keep their household goods.
